body:
## How do you manage office fitout variations?

Start with a clear agreed scope, then record each proposed change against it. Identify why the change is being requested, its cost and programme implications, which advisers need to review it and who has authority to decide. Keep a request separate from an instruction and an approved change separate from a paid invoice.

For a Newcastle business owner, the aim is visibility: what is changing, what the business has committed to and which costs or decisions remain uncertain. A single running total without those distinctions can hide a budget problem until late in the project.

Your Office Space provides client-side project management. We help coordinate the agreed brief, budget, scope, programme and client decisions. YOS does not carry out fitout construction as principal contractor. Appointed contractors, designers, certifiers and other specialist advisers retain their respective responsibilities.

[BUTTON: Discuss my Newcastle fitout budget]

**Free working pack:** [Download the two-page variation checklist (PDF)](/guides/office-fitout-variations-newcastle-checklist.pdf) or [use the editable text version](/guides/office-fitout-variations-newcastle-checklist.txt). The worksheet is a planning record. It does not authorise work, change a contract or replace the contract's notice and instruction requirements.

## Set a scope baseline you can refer back to

Keep the current agreed drawings, specification, furniture schedule, inclusions, exclusions and pricing documents together. Record their revisions and how they relate to the appointments and construction contract. Ask the relevant advisers to resolve gaps or conflicting documents.

The [fitout design brief guide](/blog/office-fitout-design-brief-newcastle) helps develop the business requirements before this stage. The [construction quote comparison guide](/blog/compare-office-construction-quotes-newcastle) helps identify pricing differences before appointment. This guide deals with controlling changes after an agreed baseline exists.

Without that baseline, a discussion about a “variation” can actually be a disagreement about what was included. If entitlement or interpretation is disputed, refer it to the appropriately appointed contract and legal advisers rather than deciding from a spreadsheet.

## Use one change register with clear statuses

| Status | What it means in the project record | What still needs to happen |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Requested | Someone has proposed a change | Confirm the request and the information needed |
| Under review | Scope, cost, timing or specialist advice is being gathered | Identify unresolved impacts and the decision owner |
| Priced, awaiting decision | A proposal is available for consideration | Check its assumptions and obtain the required decision |
| Approved and instructed | The required authority and instruction are recorded | Update the affected project documents |
| Declined or withdrawn | The proposal is not proceeding in that form | Retain the record and confirm the baseline remains clear |
| Completed and reconciled | Delivery and cost records have been reviewed under the appointments | Close outstanding records or differences |

These are suggested management labels, not a substitute for the terminology or process in the actual contract. Name the person with authority to instruct each party. Do not assume a casual comment, site conversation or worksheet entry provides that authority.

[business.gov.au's contract guidance](https://business.gov.au/people/contractors/prepare-a-contract) recommends documenting variations and understanding their effects. Building work needs attention to the relevant rules and actual agreement. Have your solicitor and appropriately appointed contract adviser confirm the notice, pricing, instruction and dispute process for your project.

## Ask for the whole effect of a change

A proposed finish substitution may affect lead time as well as price. An extra room may affect services, furniture, approvals and the programme. Ask the appointed team to identify those interfaces rather than considering the visible item in isolation.

For each proposal, record:

- The reason and a description of what changes from the baseline.
- The drawing, specification or instruction revision affected.
- Additions and omissions, including assumptions and exclusions.
- The GST basis and any unpriced elements.
- Effects on design, approvals, services, procurement and programme.
- Adviser reviews, decision authority and the recorded outcome.

Ask what depends on the decision and when it is needed. A review deadline is useful, but it should not turn an incomplete proposal into an automatically accepted instruction. Urgent, safety-related or disputed matters need the responsible parties' actual processes and advice.

## Keep contingency inside the total budget

Contingency is part of the approved project budget when the business includes it there. It should not become an extra amount added again when reporting available funds. Keep the reserve, approved changes and remaining exposure visible in one consistent model.

Consider this **hypothetical example, with all figures excluding GST**. It is arithmetic for illustration, not a Newcastle price benchmark or a recommended contingency percentage.

| Budget line | Illustrative amount |
| --- | --- |
| Original agreed works | $100,000 |
| Other known project costs | $10,000 |
| Contingency included in the approved budget | $10,000 |
| Total approved project budget | $120,000 |
| Net approved changes added to works | $5,000 |
| Current approved works plus other known costs | $115,000 |
| Additional unresolved exposure, estimated separately | $7,000 |
| Forecast including that exposure | $122,000 |

The forecast is $2,000 above the $120,000 budget. The original contingency is already within that budget. Adding another $10,000 to available funds would double count it. The unresolved $7,000 is an estimate to investigate, not an approved invoice or a certain final cost.

Real projects need a model that reflects their actual scope, agreements, allowances, approved omissions and estimates. Show the reporting date and explain whether each number is committed, approved, estimated or still unpriced. A blank line is not evidence of a zero cost.

## Review the forecast and programme together

At the agreed reporting interval, review the baseline, approved net changes, unresolved proposals and known risks with the appropriate team. Check that an allowance replaced by a confirmed price has not been counted twice, and that a proposed credit has not been treated as agreed before its status is resolved.

Keep business costs outside the construction price visible too: furniture, IT, temporary moves and other items may have separate owners. If scope reduction is being considered, have the appointed advisers review its effects before presenting it as a saving. Do not remove necessary performance or compliance provisions simply to make a total fit.

The [Newcastle fitout cost guide](/blog/commercial-fitout-cost-newcastle-2026) explains why square-metre pricing needs a defined scope. The [landlord and tenant works guide](/blog/landlord-tenant-fitout-works-newcastle) helps identify interfaces that might otherwise remain unallocated.

## Close changes through delivery and handover

After a decision, update the relevant scope, pricing and programme records. Track the completion evidence, outstanding questions and reconciliation under the actual appointments. Approval of a proposal is not proof that the work has been delivered or that every related invoice is correct.

Use the [fitout handover checklist](/blog/office-fitout-handover-checklist) to connect approved changes with current drawings, relevant operating information and outstanding items. Keep a record of declined and superseded proposals as well, so they are not mistaken for the final scope.

## Your Newcastle fitout variation checklist

- Record the agreed scope and pricing baseline with revisions.
- Confirm decision and instruction authority under the appointments.
- Give each proposed change a unique reference and status.
- Describe the reason and the difference from the baseline.
- Request additions, omissions, assumptions and exclusions.
- Record GST treatment and unpriced elements consistently.
- Obtain relevant design, services, approval and contract advice.
- Show programme and procurement implications.
- Record the required decision and instruction separately.
- Update approved costs, remaining reserve and unresolved exposure.
- Check allowances, credits and contingency for double counting.
- Reconcile delivery evidence and current documents at handover.

## Keep the client decision clear

YOS can help organise the change register, reporting and client decisions within an agreed project management scope. Our role is client-side coordination; authority to instruct, contract administration functions and technical responsibilities must be established in the actual appointments.

[Explore Newcastle office fitout project management with YOS](/office-fitout). Tell us your project stage, current scope documents and the changes or budget questions you are trying to resolve.

## Common questions

### What is a fitout variation?

It is a change to the agreed scope or contract arrangements. Record the baseline, proposed difference and the required review and instruction process. Whether an item is a valid variation or an entitlement question may need contract and legal advice.

### Does a change register authorise the contractor to proceed?

No. A register is a management record. Confirm who has authority and how instructions and notices must be given under the actual contract and appointments.

### How much contingency should a Newcastle office fitout have?

There is no universal percentage in this guide. The reserve should reflect the actual scope, investigations, project risks and business budget, informed by the appointed team. Record what it covers and avoid counting it twice.

### Can YOS guarantee that the fitout will not exceed budget?

No budget outcome is guaranteed. Under an agreed client-side scope, YOS can help keep scope, cost information, programme dependencies and client decisions visible. Unresolved costs and project-specific risks still need assessment.

*General business project-planning information only. Confirm design, approvals, safety, lease and contract requirements with the appropriately appointed advisers for the actual project. Scope, fees, timing and availability are agreed individually.*
